newsitem.title: INDIA: India says closely following Afghan situation.
newsitem.headline: India says closely following Afghan situation.

text.p: India, wary of rising Moslem fundamentalism in nearby Central Asia, on Monday reacted cautiously to the Taleban Islamic militia's weekend victories in Afghanistan.
"We are watching the situation very carefully," a Foreign Ministry spokesman said.

"The situation is entirely within the domestic sphere of Afghanistan. The government would like to reaffirm that it is for the Afghan people to decide on their future, free from outside influence and interference," the Foreign Ministry later said in a statement.

The Taleban movement at the weekend tightened its grip on northern Afghanistan and won vital diplomatic recognition from Pakistan as routed opposition warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum fled to Turkey.
Asked if India was prepared to follow Pakistan's lead and recognise the Taleban, the Foreign Ministry spokesman said: "We don't recognise governments. We only recognise states."
India has repeatedly called for an end to foreign interference in Afghanistan and accused arch-foe Pakistan of aiding Taleban warriors. Pakistan says it is neutral.
Iran, a key neighbour, said it was not yet ready to recognise the Taleban and would wait until the United Nations recognised the government in Kabul.
Russia and its Central Asian allies, alarmed at the spread of Islamic fundamentalism, expressed concern and tightened border security against a possible flood of refugees.
Since the Taleban swept into Kabul last September, New Delhi has expressed concern over the rise of religious fundamentalism in Central Asia.

"The government of India wishes to see reconciliation between all the different Afghan groups and the emergence of a peaceful and stable Afghanistan. This would be in the interest of the Afghan people and would benefit the entire region," the Foreign Ministry statement said.

The Taleban have frequently accused India, along with Russia and Iran, of supporting the forces of ousted Afghan President Burhanuddin Rabbani, who was driven from Kabul last September when the Taleban took the city.
The Taleban criticised India in April when it hosted a ministerial meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement to which a representative of Rabbani's ousted government was invited.
Last November, Indian Prime Minster Inder Kumar Gujral, who at that time was foreign minister, said India continued to recognise Rabbani and accused Pakistan of trying to "destabilise" Afghanistan.
The widow of former Afghan president Najibullah, who was hanged by the Taleban after they seized Kabul, lives in Delhi with family members.
